stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the office due to a persistent facial ulcer for the past 2 months.  On physical examination, the skin in sun-exposed areas is dry and rough with numerous freckles and erythematous macules.  Biopsy of the ulcerated lesion shows squamous cell carcinoma.  Further testing leads to a diagnosis of xeroderma pigmentosum.  A defect in which of the following enzymes is most likely causing this patient's condition?​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌
explanation:
Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by hypersensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation due to defective nucleotide excision repair.

UV radiation induces the formation of pyrimidine (usually thymine) dimers, covalently bonded intrastrand cross-links between adjacent bases that distort the double helix and inhibit DNA replication beyond the site of dimerization.  Nucleotide excision repair normally removes these lesions through a series of enzymatic steps:

  • First, the distortion is recognized and helicase unwinds the surrounding DNA, after which endonucleases cut the damaged strand on either side of the lesion and the segment containing the dimer is excised.

  • Next, DNA polymerase fills the resulting gap, using the opposing strand as a template.

  • Finally, DNA ligase seals the remaining nick, linking the new segment to existing DNA.

XP results from mutations that impair the early, lesion-specific steps of nucleotide excision repair, such as those that recognize the distorted helix and incise the damaged strand (eg, endonuclease).  Defective repair allows UV-induced DNA damage to accumulate, producing severe photosensitivity and a mutation burden that drives cutaneous malignancy in childhood (as in this patient).

(Choice A)  During DNA replication, DNA polymerase uses 3′→5′ exonuclease ("proofreading") activity to recognize, excise, and replace incorrectly paired bases.  DNA polymerase does participate in nucleotide excision repair, but only by filling the gap after excision; its proofreading activity is not involved.

(Choice B)  DNA glycosylase initiates base excision repair by cleaving the N-glycosidic bond of a damaged base, which is typically the product of spontaneous deamination, oxidation, or alkylation rather than UV exposure.  Recognition and excision of UV-induced dimers are instead performed by nucleotide excision repair machinery.

(Choice C)  DNA ligase seals the remaining nick after the gap is filled with newly synthesized DNA, a terminal step shared by nucleotide excision repair, base excision repair, mismatch repair, and DNA replication.  However, ligase acts downstream of the recognition and incision steps that are impaired in XP, and ligase deficiency does not cause this disorder.

(Choice E)  Topoisomerase relieves the supercoiling generated when helicase unwinds DNA and is not involved in the pathogenesis of XP.  Prokaryotic topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase) is inhibited by fluoroquinolones, whereas eukaryotic topoisomerase II is inhibited by etoposide.

Educational objective:Xeroderma pigmentosum (severe photosensitivity, early-onset cutaneous malignancies) is caused by defective nucleotide excision repair, which allows ultraviolet radiation–induced DNA damage (eg, thymine dimers) to accumulate.  Causes include mutations that impair recognition of the distorted DNA helix and endonuclease-mediated excision of the damaged segment.​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌
